geelong.intro: Victoria’s second-largest city wraps around Corio Bay, an hour down the highway from Melbourne. The waterfront is the place to start: a long, walkable foreshore with the painted Baywalk Bollards, swimming enclosures and bay views. It’s also the gateway to the Bellarine Peninsula and the start of the Great Ocean Road country, so it works as a base or a first stop.

ballarat.intro: Ballarat grew rich in the 1850s gold rush, and it shows: grand Victorian streetscapes along Lydiard and Sturt streets, ornate arcades and old hotels. Sovereign Hill, the outdoor museum recreating a gold-rush town, is the big drawcard, and Lake Wendouree with its botanical gardens is made for an easy afternoon.

bendigo.intro: Another gold-rush city, Bendigo pairs grand 19th-century architecture with a serious arts scene. The Bendigo Art Gallery punches well above its weight with touring exhibitions, the Golden Dragon Museum tells the story of the city’s Chinese community, and you can head underground at the Central Deborah Gold Mine.

daylesford.intro: Daylesford and neighbouring Hepburn Springs sit in Victoria’s spa country, on the largest concentration of mineral springs in Australia. Come for the bathhouses and a slow weekend: Lake Daylesford, Wombat Hill Botanic Gardens, galleries, produce stores and long lunches in the surrounding hills.

bright.intro: Bright sits in the Ovens Valley at the foot of Mount Buffalo, the classic High Country base. Autumn turns the town’s European trees gold and red, the Murray to Mountains Rail Trail runs right through it, and the alpine resorts at Falls Creek and Mount Hotham are within a short drive in winter.

phillip-island.intro: Phillip Island is famous for the Penguin Parade at dusk, when little penguins come ashore at Summerland Beach. There’s plenty more: surf beaches, the Nobbies boardwalk and its seal colony views, koalas, and the Grand Prix motorcycle circuit. Cowes is the main town, with the cafés and most of the places to stay.

warrnambool.intro: Warrnambool sits at the western end of the Great Ocean Road. From roughly May to September, southern right whales come close to shore to calve, often visible from the viewing platform at Logans Beach. Flagstaff Hill Maritime Village tells the story of the Shipwreck Coast, and the beaches and river walks are right on the doorstep.

torquay.intro: Torquay is where the Great Ocean Road begins and where Australian surf culture took off: Rip Curl and Quiksilver both started here, and world-famous Bells Beach is just down the road. Expect surf beaches, the Australian National Surfing Museum and plenty of places to fuel up before the drive west.

st-kilda.intro: St Kilda is Melbourne’s bayside playground: the palm-lined Esplanade, Luna Park’s famous face, the cake shops of Acland Street and long sunset walks on the pier, where a colony of little penguins lives in the breakwater. It’s busy, a little scruffy and full of places to eat and drink.

mornington.intro: Mornington is the Mornington Peninsula’s main-street town, with a weekly Wednesday street market, a historic pier and the sheltered swimming at Mothers Beach. It’s the easy gateway to the peninsula’s wineries, hot springs and back beaches further south.

halls-gap.intro: Halls Gap is the village at the heart of the Grampians (Gariwerd) National Park, ringed by sandstone ranges. It’s the base for the park’s best-known walks and lookouts: the Pinnacle, MacKenzie Falls, and Boroka and Reed lookouts. Kangaroos graze the town oval at dusk, and the Brambuk cultural centre tells the story of the Jardwadjali and Djab Wurrung peoples.

dunkeld.intro: Dunkeld is a small town at the southern tip of the Grampians, under the peaks of Mount Sturgeon and Mount Abrupt. It punches far above its size for food, and the climb up Mount Sturgeon rewards you with views back across the range. It’s an easy stop between the Grampians and the coast.

port-fairy.intro: Port Fairy is a historic fishing village of whalers’ cottages, stone churches and a working harbour on the Moyne River. Walk out to the lighthouse on Griffiths Island, home to a shearwater colony, and time a visit for the Port Fairy Folk Festival in March if you like a crowd.

port-campbell.intro: Port Campbell is the small coastal town closest to the Twelve Apostles. Loch Ard Gorge, the Arch and London Bridge are all a short drive away along the Port Campbell National Park coastline. Stay the night so you can see the limestone stacks at sunset and again at sunrise, without the daytime crowds.

apollo-bay.intro: Apollo Bay is a fishing town where the Great Ocean Road meets the Otway Ranges. Head inland for rainforest walks and waterfalls in the Great Otway National Park, drive out to the Cape Otway Lightstation, or climb to Mariners Lookout for the view back over the bay.

lorne.intro: Lorne is the classic Great Ocean Road beach town, where the forest of the Otways comes right down to the sand. Swim or surf the main beach, walk out on the pier, then drive up to Teddy’s Lookout for the famous view of the road snaking along the coast, or into the hills to Erskine Falls.

wangaratta.intro: Wangaratta sits where the Ovens and King rivers meet, at the start of the Great Alpine Road. It’s the gateway to the King Valley’s Italian-heritage wineries and home to a well-known jazz and blues festival in spring.

myrtleford.intro: Myrtleford is a relaxed Ovens Valley town on the Great Alpine Road and the Murray to Mountains Rail Trail, with tobacco-kiln heritage, walnut and hop country around it, and Mount Buffalo looming to the south.

harrietville.intro: Harrietville is a tiny old gold-mining village at the foot of Mount Hotham, the last stop before the Great Alpine Road climbs into the mountains. It’s the start of the Razorback and Mount Feathertop walks for keen hikers.

do: Most visitors come for the walking. The Bungalow Spur and Razorback tracks to Mount Feathertop, Victoria's second-highest peak, start near the village; both are long, steep, full-day walks, best from late spring to autumn.

Harrietville is also the last stop before the Great Alpine Road climbs to Mount Hotham, so it's a base for the snowfields in winter and for cycling the climb in summer. Check road and track conditions with Parks Victoria before you set out.

mount-hotham.intro: Mount Hotham is one of Victoria’s highest alpine resorts, right on the Great Alpine Road. In winter it’s a ski and snowboard village; in summer the high plains open up for walking, wildflowers and huge views across the Alps. Carry chains in winter, as alpine road rules apply.

omeo.intro: Omeo is a remote high-country town on the Great Alpine Road between Hotham and Gippsland, with gold-rush history, a historic courthouse precinct and the Oriental Claims walk through old sluicing sites.

bairnsdale.intro: Bairnsdale is East Gippsland’s main town, where the Great Alpine Road meets the Princes Highway. It’s known for the painted ceiling of St Mary’s Church and makes an easy base for the Gippsland Lakes.

lakes-entrance.intro: Lakes Entrance is a seaside fishing town where the Gippsland Lakes meet Bass Strait. Walk the footbridge to Ninety Mile Beach, eat fish and chips off the trawlers and take a cruise on the lakes.

metung.intro: Metung is a small, pretty village on the shores of the Gippsland Lakes, made for boating, waterfront lunches and doing very little. It’s a short drive from Lakes Entrance and Bairnsdale.

sorrento.intro: Sorrento sits near the tip of the Mornington Peninsula, with calm bay beaches on one side and wild ocean back beaches on the other. Swim with the dolphins in summer, catch the ferry across to Queenscliff, or walk the coastal tracks of Point Nepean.

red-hill.intro: Red Hill is the peninsula’s wine and food heartland: rolling hills of cool-climate vineyards, cellar doors, orchards and a monthly community market. It’s the place for a long lunch.

dromana.intro: Dromana is a bayside town at the foot of Arthurs Seat. Ride the Eagle chairlift to the summit for views across Port Phillip Bay, then cool off at the beach.

flinders.intro: Flinders is a quiet village on Western Port with a historic pier, golf on the clifftops and some of the best rock-pool walks on the peninsula at Mushroom Reef.

healesville.intro: Healesville is the Yarra Valley’s main town, home to Healesville Sanctuary’s native wildlife and surrounded by wineries, a distillery and a chocolate factory. It’s an easy base for a valley day out.

yarra-glen.intro: Yarra Glen sits in the middle of the Yarra Valley wine country, close to some of the region’s best-known cellar doors, with hot-air balloon flights over the vineyards at dawn.

do: Yarra Glen is surrounded by Yarra Valley wineries, many with cellar doors and restaurants, and it's one of the main launch points for hot-air balloon flights over the valley. Flights leave around dawn and depend on the weather, so book ahead and keep a spare morning.
Healesville Sanctuary and the Yarra Valley's distilleries and dairies are a short drive away, which makes Yarra Glen an easy base for a day or two in the valley.

melbourne-cbd.intro: Melbourne’s city centre is a grid of laneways, arcades and rooftop bars, built on gold-rush money and best explored on foot. Get lost in Degraves Street and Hosier Lane, see the State Library’s domed reading room, then cross Federation Square to the river. The free tram zone covers the whole grid.

southbank.intro: Southbank runs along the south side of the Yarra opposite the city, home to the Arts Centre, the NGV International, the Melbourne Recital Centre and a riverside promenade lined with restaurants and bars. It’s Melbourne’s culture strip, an easy walk across the bridges from Flinders Street.

docklands.intro: Docklands is Melbourne’s modern waterfront on the western edge of the city, with marinas, the Marvel Stadium, a big Ferris wheel at Melbourne Star and waterside restaurants. It’s quieter than the CBD and an easy tram ride away.

south-yarra.intro: South Yarra is one of Melbourne’s busiest dining and shopping neighbourhoods, centred on Chapel Street and Toorak Road. It borders the Royal Botanic Gardens, the Prahran Market is just down the road, and evenings run late.

fitzroy.intro: Fitzroy is Melbourne’s original bohemian inner suburb: Brunswick and Gertrude streets are packed with cafés, bars, vintage shops, galleries and live music. Come hungry and wander.

brunswick.intro: Brunswick stretches up Sydney Road, Lygon Street and Barkly Square, mixing Middle Eastern bakeries, old Italian cafés, breweries and live-music pubs. It’s laid-back, local and full of good cheap eats.

williamstown.intro: Williamstown is a historic seaport on Port Phillip Bay, with bluestone buildings, a waterfront of fish-and-chip shops and views straight back across the water to the city skyline. Arrive by ferry from Southbank for the full effect.

footscray.intro: Footscray is Melbourne’s most multicultural food suburb, famous for Vietnamese and East African eating around the market and Hopkins Street. It’s on the Maribyrnong River, a quick train from the city.

richmond.intro: Richmond is known for Victoria Street’s Vietnamese restaurants, the Swan Street pub strip and Bridge Road shopping. It sits right next to the MCG and the sporting precinct, so expect crowds on game days.

carlton.intro: Carlton is Melbourne’s Little Italy, centred on Lygon Street’s cafés and restaurants. It’s also home to the World Heritage-listed Royal Exhibition Building, the Melbourne Museum and the leafy Carlton Gardens.

port-melbourne.intro: Port Melbourne is a bayside suburb with a long, sandy beach, Station Pier where the Spirit of Tasmania docks, and Bay Street’s cafés and pubs. It’s a breezy walk or ride along the foreshore to St Kilda.

collingwood.intro: Collingwood is Fitzroy’s grittier neighbour, with Smith Street and Johnston Street bars, warehouse breweries, the Collingwood Yards arts precinct and plenty of places to eat late.

mildura.intro: Mildura is the Murray River’s big oasis town in Victoria’s far north-west, with year-round sunshine, paddlesteamers, irrigated vineyards and citrus groves. It’s a base for Mungo National Park and the Murray’s houseboats.

echuca.intro: Echuca was once Australia’s largest inland port, and its historic wharf still runs the world’s largest fleet of paddlesteamers. Cruise the Murray, explore the port precinct and stay a night on a houseboat.

shepparton.intro: Shepparton is the main city of the Goulburn Valley food bowl, known for orchards, the Shepparton Art Museum (SAM) on Victoria Park Lake and its colourful public cows. It’s a handy stop between Melbourne and the Murray.

swan-hill.intro: Swan Hill sits on the Murray in Victoria’s north, home to the Pioneer Settlement, a living-history recreation of a river town, and a sound-and-light show by night.

beechworth.intro: Beechworth is one of Victoria’s best-preserved gold-rush towns, with honey-coloured granite buildings, a famous bakery, Ned Kelly history at the old courthouse and gaol, and excellent wineries close by.

falls-creek.intro: Falls Creek is a ski-in, ski-out alpine village on the Bogong High Plains. Winters bring snow sports; summers bring mountain biking, walking on the high plains and the Rocky Valley lakes.

castlemaine.intro: Castlemaine is a creative goldfields town of galleries, op shops, the Theatre Royal and the old Mill precinct, with the heritage steam train running to Maldon at weekends.

inverloch.intro: Inverloch is a relaxed South Gippsland beach town on Anderson Inlet, with safe swimming, surf at the main beach, rock pools and the dinosaur fossil site at Flat Rocks. It’s the gateway to the Bunurong coast drive.

ocean-grove.intro: Ocean Grove is a surf and family beach town on the Bellarine Peninsula, with patrolled beaches, the Barwon River estuary and easy access to Barwon Heads and the Bellarine wineries.

queenscliff.intro: Queenscliff is a heritage seaside town at the tip of the Bellarine Peninsula, with grand Victorian hotels, Fort Queenscliff and the car ferry across the bay to Sorrento.

rye.intro: Rye is a classic Mornington Peninsula beach town with calm bay beaches and a long pier on one side and the wild ocean back beach on the other. The Peninsula Hot Springs are a short drive away.

anglesea.intro: Anglesea is a relaxed surf town at the start of the Great Ocean Road, about 20 minutes past Torquay. Kangaroos graze on the local golf course, and the river mouth and main beach suit families.

eat: Anglesea's food is casual beach-town eating: cafés for coffee after a surf, a pub, and a handful of restaurants. On our list that includes the Anglesea Pub, Coast Side Cafe, Cannoli 73 and Minerva & the Bean, plus Morgans Bar & Grill, Umisango, Love House Anglesea and Anglesea Pizza & Pasta for dinner.
Summer weekends and school holidays get busy along the Great Ocean Road, so book ahead for dinner then; in the quieter months some places shorten their hours.

kyneton.intro: Kyneton is a bluestone town in the Macedon Ranges, about an hour north-west of Melbourne, known for Piper Street's restaurants, cafés and antique shops. The Botanic Gardens and the Campaspe River walk are close to the centre.

mansfield.intro: Mansfield is the High Country town at the foot of Mount Buller: a base for skiing in winter and for Lake Eildon, horse riding and mountain biking the rest of the year. It has a lively main street of pubs and cafés for its size.

warburton.intro: Warburton sits on the Upper Yarra River at the end of the Lilydale to Warburton Rail Trail, a popular, mostly flat bike ride. The Redwood Forest at East Warburton and the Mount Donna Buang lookout are nearby.

barwon-heads.intro: Barwon Heads is a small seaside village at the mouth of the Barwon River on the Bellarine Peninsula, with a well-known river bridge, calm river beaches and the surf of Thirteenth Beach.

marysville.intro: Marysville is a mountain village about 90 minutes north-east of Melbourne, rebuilt after the 2009 Black Saturday bushfires. Steavenson Falls, one of Victoria's tallest waterfalls, is a short walk from town, and Lake Mountain has cross-country skiing in winter.

eat: Marysville is small, so eating out mostly means the cafés and bakery in the village centre plus a couple of pubs. On our list that includes the Marysville Country Bakery, Keppel Cafe, Fraga's Cafe and Freshly Blended for breakfast and lunch, and the Crossways Historic Country Inn and The Duck Inn for a pub meal.
It's a day-trip town, and many places keep daytime hours or close early midweek, so check opening times before you rely on dinner, especially outside weekends and the snow season.

brighton.intro: Brighton is a bayside suburb about 11 km south-east of the CBD, known for the colourful bathing boxes on Dendy Street Beach and the shops and cafés of Church Street and Bay Street.

rutherglen.intro: Rutherglen is a wine town near the Murray River in north-east Victoria, famous for fortified muscat and topaque from old family wineries. Its main street keeps many of its gold-era buildings.

belgrave.intro: Belgrave is the gateway to the Dandenong Ranges and the home station of Puffing Billy, the century-old steam railway. Sherbrooke Forest and the Dandenong Ranges National Park walks are minutes away.

collections.name: Day trips from Melbourne
collections.intro: Places close enough to see in a day and be home for dinner, all within about two hours of the city.

collections.name: Weekend getaways from Melbourne
collections.intro: Worth a night or two: further afield, or simply too good to rush.
body: Two nights is right for anywhere two to three hours from Melbourne: leave on Friday afternoon, have a full Saturday and drive home on Sunday.

School holidays and long weekends book out early in the coastal and alpine towns, so find a place to stay first. In winter, the Great Ocean Road and the High Country are quieter and cheaper; summer is peak season on the coast.

collections.name: Beaches and coast
collections.intro: Surf breaks, sheltered bays and coastal walks, from the city’s edge to the Shipwreck Coast.

collections.name: Gold rush towns
collections.intro: The 1850s gold rush built some of Victoria’s grandest towns. Come for the streetscapes, museums and history.
body: Gold was found near Ballarat and Bendigo in 1851, the same year Victoria became a separate colony. Within ten years the population had grown several times over, and the money built the stone banks, town halls, hotels and wide streetscapes these towns still have.

The diggers came from everywhere. Many travelled from Britain and Ireland, others from Europe and North America, and tens of thousands came from southern China. Their stories are told in places like Bendigo’s Golden Dragon Museum and Ballarat’s Eureka Centre, which covers the 1854 Eureka Stockade, a miners’ rebellion over licence fees that became a landmark in Australian democracy.

Ballarat, Castlemaine and Bendigo sit in a loose ring 100 to 130 km north-west of Melbourne and make an easy two- or three-day loop by car or V/Line train. Beechworth, in the north-east, is further but is one of the best-preserved gold towns in the state. Daylesford grew up on the diggings too, though most people now come for the mineral springs.

How long to spend: Ballarat and Bendigo each deserve a full day, Daylesford is best with a night so you can enjoy the spa without rushing, and Castlemaine and Beechworth can be done in half a day each. Two nights is enough to see the central goldfields properly, three if you want to slow down, eat well and add the smaller towns. Beechworth works better as part of a north-east trip with Rutherglen and Bright.

What to look for: the grand public buildings in each town’s centre, verandahed shopfronts on the main streets, miners’ cottages on the side streets, and the botanical gardens that most gold towns planted when they got rich. Many towns also have heritage walks with signs explaining the history.

Beyond the big names: smaller towns such as Maldon, Clunes, Talbot and Maryborough are worth a look if you like quiet streets and old buildings. Clunes is known for its book town festival, Maldon for its intact streetscape, and Talbot for its monthly farmers market.

Getting around: Ballarat, Castlemaine, Kyneton and Bendigo are all on V/Line train lines from Southern Cross, and the town centres are walkable once you arrive. Daylesford is reached by coach from Ballarat or Woodend. A car makes it easier to reach smaller places like Maldon, Clunes and Talbot, and to link the towns in a loop.

When to go: autumn is the classic season, when the European trees in the gardens turn, but spring is lovely too. Inland summers can be hot. For a ready-made plan, try our four-day Goldfields Road Trip, which links Ballarat, Daylesford, Castlemaine and Bendigo.

notes.ballarat: Victoria’s biggest inland city and the heart of the gold rush. Sovereign Hill recreates an 1850s goldfields town, the Eureka Centre tells the story of the 1854 Eureka Stockade, and Lydiard Street keeps its boom-era banks and hotels. The Art Gallery of Ballarat and the gardens on Lake Wendouree round out a full day.
notes.bendigo: Grand gold-boom buildings, underground tours at the Central Deborah Gold Mine, the Golden Dragon Museum on the town’s Chinese heritage and the Bendigo Art Gallery, known for its major touring exhibitions. The Talking Tram is an easy way to see the city.
notes.castlemaine: A smaller gold town with heritage streets, the botanical gardens and a lively café and art scene around the old Castlemaine Mill. A steam train runs on some days on the Victorian Goldfields Railway to nearby Maldon, one of the best-preserved gold villages in the state.
notes.beechworth: Honey-coloured granite buildings, the courthouse where Ned Kelly appeared in 1880, and a famous bakery. It sits in the north-east near Rutherglen’s wineries and the High Country, so it pairs well with a longer trip.
notes.daylesford: A goldfields town turned spa town, with Hepburn Springs next door. Taste the mineral springs from the hand pumps, soak at the Hepburn Bathhouse, walk around Lake Daylesford and browse the galleries. It’s about 45 minutes from Ballarat.

collections.name: Food and wine weekends
collections.intro: Long lunches, cellar doors and produce stores. Towns where eating well is the main event.
body: Victoria's wine regions are close to the city. The Yarra Valley is about an hour east of Melbourne and the Mornington Peninsula about an hour south, so both work as a day trip or an easy overnight stay. Further out, the High Country around Bright and Beechworth pairs cellar doors with alpine produce.
Book long lunches ahead on weekends, and plan a designated driver or a winery tour: many cellar doors are on winding country roads.

notes.daylesford: Bakeries, produce stores and restaurants around Lake Daylesford and Hepburn Springs.
notes.yarra-glen: In the middle of the Yarra Valley, minutes from some of its best-known cellar doors, with balloon flights over the vineyards at dawn.
notes.healesville: Yarra Valley cellar doors, a gin distillery and local cheese, with Healesville Sanctuary for a break between tastings.
notes.red-hill: The heart of the Mornington Peninsula's cool-climate wine country: pinot noir, chardonnay and cellar-door restaurants.
notes.mornington: Main Street cafés and restaurants, with the Peninsula's wineries a short drive inland.
notes.bright: The gateway to the Alpine Valleys wineries and breweries, with bakeries and farm gates along the Great Alpine Road.
notes.beechworth: A gold town with a strong food scene: a famous bakery, honey and wineries in the surrounding hills.
notes.geelong: Waterfront dining, with the Bellarine and Moorabool Valley wineries close by.
notes.rutherglen: Fortified muscat and topaque from old family wineries near the Murray River.
notes.kyneton: Piper Street's restaurants and cafés, an hour from Melbourne in the Macedon Ranges.

collections.name: Romantic getaways in Victoria
collections.intro: Spa towns, beach towns and mountain villages made for a weekend for two.

pages.title: About Vic Tours
pages.description: Vic Tours is a town-by-town guide to Victoria, made in Melbourne.
paragraphs: Vic Tours is a town-by-town guide to Victoria: where to stay, where to eat and what to do, in one place for each town and Melbourne neighbourhood.

It's made in Melbourne by Independent Media Network Pty Ltd, a small independent publisher. We start with open data, so every listing is a real place, and add local knowledge on top: which towns pair well, how long to stay and what to book ahead.

We don't charge places to be listed and we don't rank anyone for payment. Places with fuller details (website, hours, address) come first, so the most useful listings are easiest to find. How we build the guides is explained on our methods page.
Some links may later become booking links that pay us a small commission at no cost to you. When they do, they're labelled on the page.
Spotted something wrong or missing? Most listings come from OpenStreetMap, which anyone can improve, and fixes there flow back into our guides.

pages.title: How we build our guides
pages.description: Where Vic Tours’ listings come from, how we order them and how to correct them.
paragraphs: Listings come from OpenStreetMap, the free, community-edited map of the world (© OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database Licence).
Places with more complete details (website, opening hours, address) are shown first, and chain restaurants are listed last. We don’t accept payment for placement.
Distances are measured in a straight line from Melbourne’s CBD, so the drive is longer. Opening hours change, so check with the venue before you go.
Some links may become booking links in future. If they do, we’ll say so clearly on the page.

pages.title: Contact Vic Tours
pages.description: How to contact Vic Tours: corrections, local tips and partnership enquiries.
paragraphs: We'd love to hear from you, whether it's a correction, a local tip for a town we cover, or a business enquiry.
Email: hello@victours.com.au. We read everything and usually reply within a few days.

Found a wrong or missing listing? Most places come from OpenStreetMap, so the quickest fix is to edit it there (openstreetmap.org), and the change flows into our guides. Or just email us and we'll sort it out.
Vic Tours is published by Independent Media Network Pty Ltd, Melbourne, Victoria.

pages.title: Privacy policy
pages.description: What information Vic Tours collects, how it's used and your choices.
paragraphs: Last updated: October 2026. This policy explains what information victours.com.au collects and how it's used. We collect as little as possible.

Analytics: we use Google Analytics to understand which pages are useful (pages viewed, approximate location, device and the links people click). It uses cookies. We don't use it to identify you, and we don't sell data. You can block analytics cookies in your browser or with Google's opt-out add-on.

Booking and affiliate links: some links take you to partners such as booking or tour websites. If you book, the partner may pay us a commission and will use its own cookies to record that the booking came from us. Their privacy policies apply on their sites.
Email: if you email us, we use your address only to reply.

Email list: if you sign up for our emails, we store your email address, the page you signed up on and the date, on Cloudflare's servers. We use it only to send Vic Tours emails (new trip ideas, about once a month). We never sell or share it. Every email has an unsubscribe link, or email us and we'll remove you.

Plan emails: if you ask us to email you a plan, we store your email address and which plan you asked for, send you one email with a link to it, and add you to our email list (new day trips about once a month). Every email has a one-click unsubscribe link. Emails are sent through Resend, our email provider.
We don't run accounts or take payments on this site. Questions or requests: hello@victours.com.au. Independent Media Network Pty Ltd, Melbourne, Victoria.

pages.title: Affiliate disclosure
pages.description: How Vic Tours earns money: booking links and what that means for you.
paragraphs: Vic Tours is free to use. To keep it that way, some links on the site are affiliate links: if you click through to a partner (for example a hotel booking or tour site) and book, the partner may pay us a small commission. The price you pay is the same.

Affiliate links are labelled on the page. We never charge places to be listed and never rank a place higher because it pays us: listings are ordered by how complete their details are, as explained on our methods page.
Partners may include Booking.com, Viator, GetYourGuide, Klook and car hire comparison sites.

loops.name: Western Victoria Loop
loops.summary: Seven days from Melbourne: the goldfields, the Grampians and the Great Ocean Road, home along the coast.
loops.intro: A week-long self-drive loop through three of Victoria’s best regions. You head out through the gold-rush city of Ballarat, spend two nights among the Grampians’ ranges and waterfalls, then drop south to the Shipwreck Coast and drive the Great Ocean Road back towards Melbourne. Each day is a comfortable drive with plenty of time for walks, long lunches and lookouts.

days.title: Melbourne to Ballarat
days.text: An easy 90 minutes west on the Western Freeway. Spend the afternoon at Sovereign Hill, the open-air museum that recreates a 1850s goldfields town, where you can pan for gold and watch a gold pour. Afterwards walk Lydiard and Sturt streets to see the banks, hotels and theatres the gold paid for, then loop Lake Wendouree and the botanical gardens as the sun goes down.

days.title: Ballarat to the Grampians
days.text: Head west for about an hour and three quarters through Ararat and Stawell into the Grampians. Settle into Halls Gap, the only real town inside the ranges, then drive up to Boroka Lookout or Reed Lookout for late-afternoon views over the valley and Lake Bellfield. At dusk, kangaroos graze on the town oval and around the edges of Halls Gap, so drive slowly after dark.

days.title: A day in the Grampians
days.text: A full day on foot. Start early with the walk to the Pinnacle, the park’s best-known lookout, from the Wonderland area or the longer track from town. In the afternoon drive to MacKenzie Falls: the steps down to the base are steep, but the falls run year-round and are worth it. Leave an hour for Brambuk, the National Park and Cultural Centre, to learn about Gariwerd’s Aboriginal history and rock-art sites.

days.title: The Grampians to Port Fairy
days.text: Drive south through the range on the road past the Serra Range to Dunkeld, about 45 minutes, and have lunch beneath Mount Sturgeon. Fit walkers can climb Mount Sturgeon for the view back over the Grampians. Then continue south to the coast and Port Fairy, a fishing village of bluestone cottages and old pubs. Before dinner, walk the Griffiths Island loop out to the lighthouse, about an hour.

days.title: The Shipwreck Coast
days.text: About 25 minutes along the coast is Warrnambool. In whale season, roughly May to September, southern right whales calve close to shore at Logans Beach, where there is a viewing platform. Then follow the coast east past the Bay of Islands, the Grotto and London Arch to Port Campbell. Check into town, then be at the Twelve Apostles or Loch Ard Gorge for sunset, when the limestone turns gold.

days.title: Through the Otways
days.text: Get up early and see the Apostles again at sunrise, when the coach crowds haven’t arrived. Then the road turns inland through the Otway Ranges via Lavers Hill to Apollo Bay. Break the drive with the short rainforest walk at Maits Rest, a detour to the Cape Otway Lightstation, or a waterfall such as Hopetoun Falls. After lunch in Apollo Bay, look for koalas in the trees around Kennett River, then finish on the beach at Lorne.

days.title: Lorne to Melbourne
days.text: The final day is the most famous stretch of the road. Start at Teddy’s Lookout above Lorne, then follow the cliffs past Big Hill and Eastern View, where the Memorial Arch marks the road’s history. Stop at Split Point Lighthouse at Aireys Inlet, then surf-town Torquay and Bells Beach. Melbourne is about 90 minutes from Torquay.

body: This is the trip to take if you only have one week and want to see the best of the state outside Melbourne. It strings together three very different landscapes: the gold-rush streets of Ballarat, the sandstone ranges of the Grampians (Gariwerd), and the cliffs of the Shipwreck Coast and Great Ocean Road. None of the driving days is long, so there is time to walk, swim and stop for lunch without watching the clock.

The loop runs anticlockwise on purpose. Driving the Great Ocean Road from west to east puts you on the ocean side of the road for the final stretch, which makes pulling into lookouts easier and gives the best views. It also means you finish with the most famous section, between Lorne and Torquay, rather than starting with it.

guide.heading: When to go
paragraphs: Spring (September to November) and autumn (March to May) are the best months: the Grampians wildflowers are out in spring, the weather is mild for walking, and the Great Ocean Road is quieter than in summer. Summer school holidays bring the biggest crowds and highest accommodation prices on the coast, so book well ahead. Winter is cold and wet on the coast but is whale season at Warrnambool, and the Grampians waterfalls run hardest.

guide.heading: Driving and distances
paragraphs: The full loop is roughly 800 km. The longest single day is Port Campbell to Lorne through the Otways, which is winding and slow, so leave plenty of daylight. Watch for wildlife at dawn and dusk, especially kangaroos in the Grampians. Fuel is easy to find in every overnight town, but fill up before the Otways stretch.
Parts of the Grampians have been affected by bushfires and storms in recent years, so check Parks Victoria for walk and road closures before you go.

guide.heading: Making it shorter or longer
paragraphs: Short on time? Drop the day in Ballarat and drive straight to Halls Gap, about three hours. With more time, add a second night on the coast at Port Fairy or Apollo Bay, or swap Dunkeld for a night in the wine country around Great Western.

loops.name: Great Ocean Road in 3 days
loops.summary: The classic coastal drive from Torquay to the Twelve Apostles and Port Fairy, with two nights on the road.
loops.intro: Three days is the sweet spot for the Great Ocean Road: enough time to stop at the lookouts, walk into the Otways and see the Twelve Apostles at sunset, without rushing. You drive west along the coast and come home on the faster inland highway.

days.title: Melbourne to Lorne
days.text: Leave Melbourne mid-morning and drive about 90 minutes to Torquay, the surf town where the road begins. Have a coffee, then drive out to Bells Beach, home of the famous Easter surf contest. From Anglesea the road starts to hug the cliffs. Stop at Split Point Lighthouse at Aireys Inlet, then pass under the Memorial Arch at Eastern View onto the coast road proper. Roll into Lorne in the afternoon for a swim, a walk on the pier, and Teddy’s Lookout for the view along the coast at the end of the day. If you have energy left, Erskine Falls is a short drive inland.

days.title: Lorne to the Twelve Apostles
days.text: The most dramatic and slowest stretch of the road. The coast between Lorne and Apollo Bay is all tight bends and views, so take your time. Look for wild koalas in the gums around Kennett River, then have lunch in Apollo Bay. From here the road heads inland through the Otway Ranges. Do the 30-minute Maits Rest rainforest walk among giant tree ferns, or drive out to the Cape Otway Lightstation. Keep going to Port Campbell, check in, and be at the Twelve Apostles or Loch Ard Gorge for sunset. Gibson Steps lets you walk down onto the beach beneath the cliffs.

days.title: Port Campbell to Port Fairy and home
days.text: Get up early and see the Apostles again at sunrise, before the crowds. After breakfast in Port Campbell, follow the coast west past the Arch, London Arch (it lost its other span in 1990) and the Grotto, then the quieter Bay of Islands. Have lunch in Warrnambool, where southern right whales calve at Logans Beach roughly May to September. Finish in Port Fairy with a walk around Griffiths Island to the lighthouse, then take the inland Princes Highway home, about three and a half hours.

body: The Great Ocean Road runs about 240 km along Victoria’s south-west coast, from Torquay to near Warrnambool. It was built by returned soldiers after the First World War and is dedicated to those who died in it, which makes it the world’s largest war memorial. Most people try to do it in a day from Melbourne. Please don’t: you would spend eight hours in the car and see the Twelve Apostles in the middle of the day with every tour coach in the state.

This plan gives it three days with two nights, which is enough to drive at an easy pace, take the short walks, and see the Apostles at both sunset and sunrise. You head west along the coast and come home on the faster inland highway, so you never drive the same road twice.

guide.heading: When to go
paragraphs: Autumn and spring are the sweet spot: mild weather, fewer cars and better accommodation prices. Summer is busy, and the road gets slow on weekends and holidays, so book your two nights early. Winter is wild and moody, which suits the Shipwreck Coast, and it’s whale season in the west.

guide.heading: Driving tips
paragraphs: Drive west to east if you can’t fit in the full loop, so you’re on the ocean side for the lookouts. Many sections are narrow and winding with few overtaking lanes. Use the pull-over bays to let faster traffic pass, and keep left: many drivers here are visitors used to driving on the right. Fill up in Apollo Bay before the Otways.

guide.heading: Where to stay
paragraphs: Lorne and Port Campbell work best as the two overnight stops because they put you close to the highlights at the right times of day. Apollo Bay is a good alternative to Lorne if you want a bigger town with more choice. Port Campbell is small, so book ahead in summer and on long weekends.

guide.heading: If you only have one day
paragraphs: If a day trip is all you can manage, be honest with yourself about what you’ll see. Drive straight to Lorne, then on to Apollo Bay for lunch and the Otways, and turn back. You’ll get the best of the cliff-top driving without the long haul to the Apostles. Or join a day tour from Melbourne so someone else does the driving while you enjoy the views.

guide.heading: With kids
paragraphs: The road suits families as long as you break up the driving. Good stops include the koalas at Kennett River, the beach and playground at Lorne, the short Maits Rest boardwalk, and the rock pools at low tide around Apollo Bay. Loch Ard Gorge has a beach, caves and a shipwreck story kids remember.

loops.name: Phillip Island day trip
loops.summary: Pelicans, seals, koalas and the Penguin Parade at dusk, in one big day from Melbourne.
loops.intro: Phillip Island is about two hours from Melbourne, and the best day there ends at dusk with the Penguin Parade. Plan the day backwards from that: arrive late morning, take it slow, and book your penguin viewing ahead in busy seasons.

days.title: Melbourne to Phillip Island and back
days.text: Drive south-east via the Monash Freeway and the Bass Highway, then cross the bridge at San Remo. Time your arrival for around midday and you can watch the pelicans being fed at the San Remo jetty. On the island, start at the Nobbies, where a boardwalk follows the cliffs and looks out to Seal Rocks, home to a big colony of Australian fur seals. In the afternoon pick one or two of the Koala Conservation Reserve, where boardwalks run through the treetops, Churchill Island’s heritage farm, or a walk at Cape Woolamai, the island’s highest point. Have a late lunch or early dinner in Cowes, the main town, on the north shore. Then head to Summerland Beach for the Penguin Parade. Arrive before sunset to get a good spot, then watch the penguins waddle up the beach to their burrows. Photography of the penguins is not allowed, to protect them. Drive home after dark.

body: Phillip Island sits at the mouth of Western Port, about two hours south-east of Melbourne by car. It’s best known for the Penguin Parade, where little penguins, the world’s smallest penguin species, come ashore at dusk. But the island has a lot more than penguins: a seal colony, koalas, surf beaches and a heritage farm on its own little island.

The trick to a good day is to plan it backwards from sunset. The Penguin Parade happens at dusk all year round, which means late in the evening in summer and in the late afternoon in winter. Aim to arrive on the island in the late morning, fill the afternoon with the other sights, and save the penguins for last.

guide.heading: Booking the Penguin Parade
paragraphs: Tickets often sell out in summer, school holidays and long weekends, so book ahead. There are several viewing options, from general beach stands to smaller guided tours and underground viewing. Dress warmly whatever the season: it gets cold and windy on the beach after sunset, even in summer.

guide.heading: Getting there
paragraphs: Driving is by far the easiest way, as public transport to the island is slow and the sights are spread out. Allow two hours each way and expect a slow drive home in the dark, watching out for wildlife on the road. Many day tours run from Melbourne too, which saves you the late drive.

guide.heading: Making it a weekend
paragraphs: If you would rather not drive back at night, stay over in Cowes. Next morning you can walk the surf beaches on the south side of the island, visit the Grand Prix circuit, or continue along the coast to Inverloch, which is the start of our Gippsland coast road trip.

guide.heading: With kids
paragraphs: This is one of the best family days out from Melbourne. Kids love the pelican feeding, the koala boardwalks and of course the penguins. Bring snacks, warm layers and something to keep them busy while you wait for the parade to start, as you may sit on the stands for half an hour or more. Some ticket options include a guided ranger talk, which helps younger children stay engaged.

guide.heading: Beaches and surf
paragraphs: The island’s south coast faces Bass Strait and has strong surf, with beaches like Woolamai and Smiths Beach popular with surfers. Swim only at patrolled beaches between the flags in summer. The north shore around Cowes faces Western Port and is much calmer, which makes it the better choice for young swimmers.

guide.heading: Wildlife on the island
paragraphs: Phillip Island is a nature park as much as a holiday spot, and much of the island’s coast is protected. As well as penguins, seals and koalas, look out for wallabies, Cape Barren geese grazing in the paddocks, and short-tailed shearwaters, which arrive in their thousands each spring after flying from the North Pacific. Stick to the boardwalks and paths, as penguin burrows are often hidden in the dunes, and drive slowly around the Summerland Peninsula, where penguins sometimes cross the road. Check under your car before you leave the penguin car park.

loops.name: The Great Alpine Road
loops.summary: Wangaratta to the Gippsland Lakes over the top of Mount Hotham, one of Australia’s highest sealed roads.
loops.intro: The Great Alpine Road runs over 300 km from Wangaratta to Bairnsdale, climbing through the Ovens Valley and over Mount Hotham before dropping through the high country to the Gippsland Lakes. Allow four days with time for walks and long lunches. In winter, carry snow chains between Harrietville and Omeo, as alpine road rules apply.

days.title: Melbourne to Bright
days.text: Drive up the Hume Freeway to Wangaratta, about two and a half hours, then turn onto the Great Alpine Road and follow the Ovens Valley south-east. The Milawa area just off the road is known for its wineries, cheese and local produce, and makes a good lunch stop. Continue through Myrtleford, where the valley starts to narrow, and arrive in Bright in time for a walk along the Ovens River. Bright is at its best in autumn, when the town’s planted trees turn red and gold.

days.title: A day around Bright
days.text: A full day to explore. Hire a bike and ride part of the Murray to Mountains Rail Trail, which runs mostly flat through the valley towards Porepunkah and Myrtleford. Or drive up to Mount Buffalo National Park for the gorge lookouts and the granite tors around the Horn. In the afternoon, work your way through the valley’s breweries and cellar doors. Wandiligong, a few minutes from Bright, is a pretty old gold-mining hamlet.

days.title: Over the mountain to Omeo
days.text: The big day. From Bright, drive to Harrietville at the foot of the mountain, then start the climb. The road twists up through snow gums to Mount Hotham, with lookouts along the way over the Victorian Alps. Stop at Dinner Plain, an alpine village just past Hotham, for coffee or lunch. Then the road drops down through the high plains and forest to Omeo, a small gold-rush town with historic buildings and a quiet main street. Check road conditions before you set off if you are travelling in winter.

days.title: Omeo to the Gippsland Lakes
days.text: Follow the Tambo Valley down from the mountains to Bairnsdale, about two hours, then turn east to the Gippsland Lakes. Have lunch on the water at Metung, a pretty village on Bancroft Bay. Finish at Lakes Entrance, where you can have fish and chips by the water and walk the footbridge over to Ninety Mile Beach for sunset. Melbourne is about four hours home the next day along the Princes Highway.

body: The Great Alpine Road is one of Australia’s great drives. It runs for more than 300 km from Wangaratta in the north-east to Bairnsdale in East Gippsland, climbing over the shoulder of Mount Hotham at more than 1,800 metres along the way. In a few days you go from the vineyards and orchards of the Ovens Valley, over the alpine high plains, down through the old gold town of Omeo and out to the Gippsland Lakes on the coast.

Allow four days so that each drive is short and you have a full day around Bright. The road is sealed the whole way, so a normal car is fine outside the snow season. In winter it becomes a different trip, with snow on the mountain and chains to carry, so read the notes below before you go.

guide.heading: Driving in winter
paragraphs: During the declared snow season, roughly June to early October, you must carry snow chains on the road between Harrietville and Omeo, and a resort entry fee applies at Mount Hotham. Snow and ice can close the road at short notice. Check VicTraffic and the Mount Hotham resort before you set off, and allow extra time.

guide.heading: When to go
paragraphs: Autumn (March to May) is the classic time, for the colours around Bright and comfortable walking weather. Late spring and summer are good for the high plains, with wildflowers on the mountain and warm days by the river. Winter suits skiers and snow lovers, as long as you’re prepared for alpine driving.

guide.heading: Doing it in reverse
paragraphs: The road works just as well from east to west. If you’re coming from Gippsland, start at Lakes Entrance and finish in Bright, then head home down the Hume.

guide.heading: Food and drink along the way
paragraphs: The Ovens Valley and the King Valley next door are among the best food and wine areas in regional Victoria. Look for cool-climate wines and Italian varieties in the King Valley, local cheese and produce around Milawa, craft beer and cider around Bright, and fresh trout and berries in the summer months. Down on the Gippsland Lakes, the seafood is the reason to stop.

loops.name: Mornington Peninsula day trip
loops.summary: Bay beaches, a chairlift ride, a winery lunch and the wild back beaches, about an hour from Melbourne.
loops.intro: The Mornington Peninsula packs bay beaches, wine country and wild ocean coastline into one easy loop from Melbourne. Drive down the bay side, cross the hills for lunch, and come home via Western Port.

days.title: A loop around the peninsula
days.text: Drive down the Peninsula Link to Mornington, about an hour, for coffee and a wander along Main Street and down to the harbour and the pier. Follow the bay to Dromana and ride the Arthurs Seat Eagle, a gondola that runs from the bottom of the hill to the summit, with wide views over the bay. Then head into the hills around Red Hill for a long lunch at one of the many cellar doors, which specialise in cool-climate pinot noir and chardonnay. In the afternoon drive down to Sorrento at the tip of the peninsula. Walk the main street, then cross to the ocean side for the rock pools and cliffs of Sorrento back beach. With time to spare, Point Nepean National Park has old forts and huge views. Head home along the Western Port side via Flinders, where you can walk out on the pier or explore the rock pools of Mushroom Reef Marine Sanctuary at low tide. Cape Schanck lighthouse and its boardwalk are a short detour on the way.

body: The Mornington Peninsula curls around the south-east side of Port Phillip Bay, about an hour from Melbourne. In one day you can swim at a calm bay beach, ride a gondola over Arthurs Seat, have lunch at a cellar door and walk on the wild ocean beaches facing Bass Strait. It’s Melbourne’s favourite summer escape for good reason.

This loop drives down the bay side in the morning, crosses the hills for lunch, reaches the tip of the peninsula in the afternoon and comes home past Western Port. If you only want one region from Melbourne in a single day, this is the easiest to plan.

guide.heading: Making the most of the day
paragraphs: Book a winery lunch in advance on weekends, especially in summer. If you plan to taste, have a designated driver or join a winery tour, as Victoria’s drink-driving limits are strictly enforced. The Arthurs Seat Eagle and some beaches get very busy on hot weekends, so arrive early.

guide.heading: Hot springs and the ferry
paragraphs: Peninsula Hot Springs at Fingal, near Rye, is one of the area’s most popular attractions, with geothermal pools set in the landscape. Book ahead, as sessions sell out. The car ferry between Sorrento and Queenscliff crosses the mouth of the bay in about 40 minutes, so you can link this trip with the Bellarine Peninsula and the start of the Great Ocean Road.

guide.heading: When to go
paragraphs: Summer is peak season, with warm days for the bay beaches but heavy traffic on weekends. Spring and autumn are quieter and great for wineries and walks. In winter the back beaches are dramatic, the cellar doors have fires going, and the hot springs are at their best.

guide.heading: Bay side or ocean side
paragraphs: The peninsula has two very different coasts. The bay beaches, from Mornington through Rosebud to Sorrento, are calm, shallow and good for swimming and paddleboarding, with colourful bathing boxes along the sand. The ocean beaches, facing Bass Strait from Portsea to Gunnamatta, have big surf, strong currents and rips. They’re stunning for walking, but only swim at patrolled ocean beaches between the flags.

guide.heading: With kids
paragraphs: Families can easily fill the day with the bay beaches, the Arthurs Seat Eagle and the maze gardens and berry farms around the hills. Berry picking is a summer favourite in the Red Hill and Main Ridge area. Many cellar doors also welcome children and have lawns to run around on, so a winery lunch doesn’t have to be adults only.

guide.heading: Walks worth doing
paragraphs: The peninsula has some excellent coastal walks. The Two Bays Walking Track runs about 26 km from Dromana on the bay to Cape Schanck on the ocean, and you can walk shorter sections of it. The Coppins Track at Sorrento follows the clifftops above the bay, and the boardwalk at Cape Schanck leads down to the rocks below the lighthouse. Point Nepean has walking and cycling tracks to the forts and the narrow entrance to the bay.

loops.name: Yarra Valley day trip
loops.summary: Native wildlife, cellar doors and a long lunch, about an hour from Melbourne.
loops.intro: The Yarra Valley is Melbourne’s closest wine region, and it’s easy to fill a day with wildlife, wineries and food. If you’re tasting, book a driver or tour.

days.title: Healesville and the valley
days.text: Leave Melbourne early and drive out along the Maroondah Highway to Healesville, about an hour. Start at Healesville Sanctuary, run by Zoos Victoria, which only keeps Australian animals. Look for koalas, kangaroos, wombats, dingoes and the platypus in its own house, and catch the free-flying birds of prey show if it’s running that day. Allow two to three hours. Then have a coffee on Healesville’s main street before driving on to the cellar doors. The valley has dozens of wineries, from big names with restaurants to small family producers, so pick two or three around Yarra Glen and Coldstream and book a long lunch at one of them. On the way home, stop at the Yarra Valley Chocolaterie near Yarra Glen or the Yarra Valley Dairy for cheese to take home.

body: The Yarra Valley is Melbourne’s closest wine region, about an hour north-east of the city. It’s known for cool-climate wines, particularly chardonnay, pinot noir and sparkling, and for its long lunches among the vines. But the valley also has one of the best places in the state to see native animals up close, plus a chocolate factory, a cheese shop and some lovely country towns.

This plan starts with wildlife while the animals are active, moves on to a winery lunch, and finishes with food stops on the way home. If you’re tasting wine, book a driver or a tour so everyone can enjoy the day.

guide.heading: Hot-air balloons
paragraphs: The Yarra Valley is one of the best places near Melbourne for a hot-air balloon flight. Flights leave at dawn, weather permitting, and usually finish with a champagne breakfast. It’s a big early start, so it pairs well with an overnight stay in the valley.

guide.heading: Getting around
paragraphs: You need a car or a tour, as public transport doesn’t reach most wineries. If you’re driving, it’s easiest to choose one area and stay there rather than zigzagging across the valley. Many winery restaurants require bookings, especially on weekends.

guide.heading: When to go
paragraphs: Autumn is the most beautiful time, with the vines turning gold and red after the harvest. Spring brings new growth and mild weather. Summer is busy with events and festivals, and winter is quieter, with log fires at the cellar doors.

guide.heading: Making it a weekend
paragraphs: Add the Dandenong Ranges on the way out or back, about 40 minutes from Healesville, for the tall forest, gardens and Puffing Billy steam railway. Or stay in Healesville and continue north over the Black Spur to Marysville, a mountain town surrounded by forest and waterfalls.

guide.heading: Where to eat
paragraphs: Many of the valley’s best restaurants are at wineries, with set menus or long lunches built around local produce and the cellar’s wines. For something more casual, Healesville’s main street has cafés, bakeries and a brewery or two, and many cellar doors serve tasting boards. If you want a sparkling wine experience, the valley is home to some of Australia’s best-known sparkling producers.

guide.heading: Planning your winery visits
paragraphs: With so many cellar doors, it helps to have a plan. Two or three wineries plus lunch is plenty for one day, especially if someone is driving. Some cellar doors charge a small tasting fee, which is often refunded if you buy a bottle, and some smaller producers are only open on weekends or by appointment. Check opening days before you set off. If you’d like to visit several, the area around Coldstream and Yarra Glen has many wineries close together, which cuts down on driving.

guide.heading: Towns worth a stop
paragraphs: Healesville is the valley’s main town, with cafés, a pub and the sanctuary. Yarra Glen has a grand old hotel and a racecourse, and Warburton, further east on the Yarra, is a quiet riverside town surrounded by forest with a rail trail and the Redwood Forest nearby. Each is easy to add to a day in the valley.

loops.name: Goldfields Road Trip
loops.summary: Four days through Victoria's gold-rush towns: Ballarat, Daylesford, Castlemaine and Bendigo.
loops.intro: The 1850s gold rush built Victoria's grandest country towns, and they sit in an easy loop north-west of Melbourne. This trip takes in Sovereign Hill and Ballarat's boom-era streets, a spa night in Daylesford, Castlemaine's heritage centre and Bendigo's mine and museums, with short drives between each.

days.title: Melbourne to Ballarat
days.text: About 90 minutes west on the Western Freeway. Spend the afternoon at Sovereign Hill, the open-air museum that recreates a 1850s goldfields town, with actors in costume, a working gold pour and a chance to pan for gold yourself. Across the road, the Gold Museum tells the bigger story. Then walk Lydiard and Sturt streets to see the boom-era banks, hotels and the Art Gallery of Ballarat, one of the oldest regional galleries in Australia. Loop Lake Wendouree and the botanical gardens before dinner. If you have time, the Eureka Centre tells the story of the 1854 Eureka Stockade, a miners’ rebellion against the colonial government.

days.title: Ballarat to Daylesford
days.text: A 45-minute drive north-east to spa country. Daylesford and neighbouring Hepburn Springs sit on Australia’s biggest concentration of mineral springs. Walk the track around Lake Daylesford, then fill a bottle from the hand pumps in the Hepburn Mineral Springs Reserve to taste the different springs. Book a soak at the Hepburn Bathhouse in the afternoon. Before dinner, browse the galleries and the Convent Gallery on Wombat Hill, and walk up to the lookout tower in the Wombat Hill Botanic Gardens.

days.title: Daylesford to Bendigo via Castlemaine
days.text: Stop in Castlemaine, about 30 minutes away, for its heritage streets, botanical gardens and the café and art scene around the old Castlemaine Mill. Nearby Maldon is one of the best-preserved gold towns in the state, and on some days a steam train runs between the two on the Victorian Goldfields Railway. Then continue to Bendigo, about 40 minutes. In the afternoon, go 61 metres underground on a Central Deborah Gold Mine tour, or ride the Talking Tram through the city past the Shamrock Hotel, the Post Office and the Alexandra Fountain.

days.title: Bendigo to Melbourne via Kyneton
days.text: See the Golden Dragon Museum in the morning, which tells the story of Bendigo’s Chinese community and is home to the processional dragons used in the Easter Festival. Or visit the Bendigo Art Gallery, known for its major touring exhibitions. Then head home, breaking the two-hour drive with lunch on Kyneton’s Piper Street, a row of bluestone buildings now full of cafés and restaurants. The Macedon Ranges and Hanging Rock are a short detour on the way.

body: In 1851 gold was found in central Victoria, and within a few years the region was one of the richest places on earth. People came from all over the world, including tens of thousands from China. The money built grand towns with stone banks, town halls, theatres and hotels, many of which still stand. Today the goldfields are an easy and rewarding trip from Melbourne, with short drives, great food and a lot of history.

This four-day loop visits the region’s two big cities, Ballarat and Bendigo, plus smaller towns in between. It mixes museums and mine tours with a night in Daylesford’s spa country, so it doesn’t feel like a history lesson the whole way.

guide.heading: Doing it by train
paragraphs: Ballarat, Castlemaine, Kyneton and Bendigo are all on V/Line train lines from Melbourne’s Southern Cross station, so you can do a version of this trip without a car. Daylesford is reached by coach from Ballarat or Woodend. A car gives you more freedom for Maldon and the smaller towns.

guide.heading: When to go
paragraphs: Autumn and spring are ideal, with mild days and cool nights for the spa. Winter is cold but cosy, and it’s a good time for Daylesford’s bathhouses and Ballarat’s winter light festivals. Summer can be hot inland, so plan outdoor sights for the morning. Bendigo’s Easter Festival, with its dragon procession, is one of the region’s biggest events.

guide.heading: With kids
paragraphs: This is a great trip for families. Kids can pan for gold and watch a gold pour at Sovereign Hill, go underground at the Central Deborah Gold Mine, see the dragons at the Golden Dragon Museum and ride the Talking Tram in Bendigo. Daylesford’s lake has paddleboats, and the gardens and playgrounds in every town give everyone a break from the car.

guide.heading: Food and drink
paragraphs: The goldfields have a strong food scene. Ballarat and Bendigo have a good mix of restaurants and cafés in their old buildings, Daylesford and Hepburn Springs are known for long lunches and local produce, and Castlemaine and Kyneton have become destinations for eating out. The region also has its own wineries, especially around Bendigo and the Macedon Ranges, with good cool-climate wines.

loops.name: Gippsland Coast Road Trip
loops.summary: Four days east: Phillip Island's penguins, the Bass Coast and the Gippsland Lakes.
loops.intro: A four-day loop through Victoria's east, from the penguins of Phillip Island along the Bass Coast to the lakes and Ninety Mile Beach at Lakes Entrance. The third day is the long one; the others are short drives with plenty of time on the beach.

days.title: Melbourne to Phillip Island
days.text: About two hours south-east via the Bass Highway. Cross the bridge at San Remo, where pelicans gather at the jetty around midday, then spend the afternoon on the island. Walk the boardwalk at the Nobbies, looking out to the fur seal colony at Seal Rocks, and visit a surf beach or the Koala Conservation Reserve. At dusk, watch little penguins come ashore at the Penguin Parade (book ahead, especially in summer). Stay the night in Cowes so you don’t have a late drive.

days.title: Phillip Island to Inverloch
days.text: Under an hour along the Bass Coast. Stop at the lookouts around Kilcunda and the Bunurong coast, where some of Australia’s first dinosaur fossils were found. In Inverloch, walk the surf beach and the Eagles Nest rock stack, or explore the rock platforms at low tide. If you want a bigger day, drive about 90 minutes to Wilsons Promontory: walk on Squeaky Beach, climb Mount Oberon for a view over the whole peninsula, and look for wombats around Tidal River in the late afternoon.

days.title: Inverloch to Lakes Entrance
days.text: The longest drive, about three and a half hours east through Leongatha and the farmland of South Gippsland to the Princes Highway. Have lunch in Bairnsdale, or on the water in Metung, a pretty village on the lakes with a pub and jetty. Then continue to Lakes Entrance, the main town on the Gippsland Lakes, and arrive in time to watch the sunset over the water.

days.title: Lakes Entrance to Melbourne
days.text: Spend the morning on the water. Take a lakes cruise, hire a boat, or walk the footbridge across the inlet to Ninety Mile Beach, one of the longest uninterrupted beaches in the world. The town’s fishing fleet means good fish and chips. Then drive home, about four hours, via Bairnsdale and the Princes Highway.

body: Gippsland is Victoria’s south-east, and it’s the least crowded of the big coastal regions near Melbourne. This four-day loop combines the wildlife of Phillip Island, the rugged Bass Coast, and the Gippsland Lakes, Australia’s largest network of inland waterways. It’s a trip for beaches, boats and seafood rather than museums.

The first two days are short drives, the third is the long one, and the last brings you home. If you want to see Wilsons Promontory, one of Victoria’s most loved national parks, the second day gives you the option of a big day trip there.

guide.heading: When to go
paragraphs: Summer is peak season on the coast, with warm days for swimming but busier towns and higher prices. Autumn and spring are quieter and still pleasant. In winter the coast is wild and empty, which some people love, but some lake activities run reduced hours.

guide.heading: Wilsons Promontory
paragraphs: The Prom is worth at least a full day of its own, and many people stay at Tidal River, the park’s campground and cabins, which books out months ahead in summer. If you can, add a night there between Inverloch and Lakes Entrance.

guide.heading: Swapping the route
paragraphs: This trip links up with the Great Alpine Road: instead of driving home from Lakes Entrance, head north through Bairnsdale and over Mount Hotham to Bright, then home down the Hume.

guide.heading: Food and drink
paragraphs: Gippsland is a farming region, so the produce is excellent. South Gippsland has dairy farms, cheese makers and local markets, and the coastal towns have fresh seafood, especially in Lakes Entrance, one of Victoria’s biggest fishing ports. Look for local wines and craft beer in the towns along the way too.

guide.heading: Swimming safety
paragraphs: The Bass Coast beaches and Ninety Mile Beach face the open ocean, with strong surf and rips. Swim at patrolled beaches between the flags in summer. The lakes and inlets are much calmer and better for families, paddling and fishing.

guide.heading: Getting around
paragraphs: You need a car for this trip, as the towns are spread out and public transport is limited. Fill up in the larger towns, because fuel stops can be far apart in the hills and forests between the coast and the highway. Watch for wildlife at dawn and dusk, especially kangaroos and wombats around Wilsons Promontory.

loops.name: Murray River and North-East Road Trip
loops.summary: Four days: Echuca's paddle steamers, Rutherglen's wineries and gold-era Beechworth.
loops.intro: Head north to the Murray River, follow it east to the wine town of Rutherglen, then climb into the north-east's gold country at Beechworth before driving home down the Hume. It's a good autumn or spring trip, when the north is warm but not hot.

days.title: Melbourne to Echuca
days.text: About two and a half hours north via the Calder or Northern Highway. Echuca was once Australia’s biggest inland port, where paddle steamers loaded wool and timber from all along the Murray. Walk the huge redgum wharf in the historic Port of Echuca precinct, then take a paddle steamer cruise. Echuca has one of the largest fleets of working paddle steamers in the world, some more than 100 years old. Have dinner in town or across the river in Moama.

days.title: Echuca to Rutherglen
days.text: About three hours east on the Murray Valley Highway, through the river towns of Cobram and Yarrawonga, where you can stop for a swim at a river beach or a walk along Lake Mulwala. Rutherglen is famous for its fortified wines, particularly muscat and topaque, made by family wineries that have been at it for generations. Spend the afternoon at a few cellar doors, then walk the gold-era main street.

days.title: Rutherglen to Beechworth
days.text: Under an hour south. Beechworth is one of Victoria’s best-preserved gold-rush towns, with honey-coloured granite buildings along its main streets. Visit the historic courthouse, where Ned Kelly faced a committal hearing in 1880, and the old government buildings around it. Then try the famous bakery, the Beechworth Honey shop, and the town’s walks and gorge. Nearby Chiltern and Yackandandah are worth a detour if you have time.

days.title: Beechworth to Melbourne via Wangaratta
days.text: Drive to Wangaratta, about 40 minutes, then head home down the Hume Freeway, about three hours. If you have an extra day, detour to the Milawa food and wine region, or take the Great Alpine Road to Myrtleford and Bright for the High Country. Wangaratta has long hosted a jazz and blues festival in early November, so check what’s on if you’re travelling then.

body: Victoria’s northern border is the Murray River, Australia’s longest. This four-day loop heads north to the old river port of Echuca, follows the Murray east to the wine town of Rutherglen, then climbs into the north-east’s gold country at Beechworth before coming home down the Hume Freeway. It’s a trip of paddle steamers, fortified wines, granite towns and long lunches.
It’s best in autumn and spring, when the north is warm but not hot. Summer days on the Murray often top 35°C, which is great for the river but tiring for sightseeing.

guide.heading: When to go
paragraphs: Autumn (March to May) is ideal, with harvest season in the wineries and mild days. Spring is also good. In summer, plan your river time for mornings and late afternoons. Winter is cool and quiet, with cosy cellar doors and fires in the pubs.

guide.heading: Wine tasting
paragraphs: Rutherglen’s wineries are spread out but close to town, and bikes are available for hire if you’d rather not drive between them. As always, if you’re tasting, have a designated driver or join a tour.

guide.heading: On the river
paragraphs: There’s more to the Murray than paddle steamers. Many river towns have sandy river beaches for swimming in summer, and you can hire a kayak, a tinny or even a houseboat for a few days. Take care in the water, as the river has strong currents and submerged snags, and always check local conditions before you swim.

guide.heading: With kids
paragraphs: Kids love the paddle steamers in Echuca and the river beaches along the way. In Beechworth, the old gaol and courthouse bring the Ned Kelly story to life, and the town’s sweets shop and bakery are a hit. Make sure everyone gets a turn in the front seat, as the longest drive is the second day.

guide.heading: Getting around
paragraphs: You need a car for this trip, as the towns are spread out and most of the drive follows country highways. Distances are longer than on the coastal trips, so plan fuel stops in the bigger towns. The drives are flat and straight in the north, then become hillier around Beechworth. Watch for kangaroos at dawn and dusk on the country roads.

regions.name: Mornington Peninsula
regions.label: Mornington Peninsula
regions.intro: The Mornington Peninsula curls around the south-east of Port Phillip Bay, about an hour from Melbourne. Calm bay beaches line one side and wild ocean beaches the other, and the hills in between hold cellar doors, berry farms and the Peninsula Hot Springs.
body: The bay-side towns (Mornington, Dromana, Rye and Sorrento) suit families and swimming. The back beaches and the Cape Schanck coast are for walking and views rather than swimming. Red Hill and Main Ridge are the food and wine heart of the peninsula.
Summer weekends and school holidays are busy, so book a place to stay early. The Searoad car ferry from Sorrento to Queenscliff makes it easy to combine the peninsula with the Bellarine.

regions.name: Yarra Valley
regions.label: Yarra Valley
regions.intro: The Yarra Valley is Victoria's best-known wine region, about an hour north-east of Melbourne, with dozens of cellar doors, Healesville Sanctuary, hot-air balloon flights at dawn and the Lilydale to Warburton Rail Trail.
body: Most visitors base themselves in Healesville or Yarra Glen. Cellar doors are quieter on weekdays; on weekends, book lunches ahead and plan a designated driver or a winery tour.
Warburton, at the end of the rail trail, adds rainforest walks and the Redwood Forest, and in winter Mount Donna Buang sometimes gets snow.

regions.name: Great Ocean Road
regions.label: Great Ocean Road
regions.intro: The Great Ocean Road runs about 240 km along Victoria's south-west coast from Torquay to near Warrnambool, past surf beaches, rainforest and the limestone stacks of the Twelve Apostles.
body: Allow at least three days to drive it properly: the road is winding and the best stops (Lorne, Apollo Bay, the Otways and the Shipwreck Coast) deserve time. Most people drive west from Melbourne and return inland on the faster Princes Highway.
See the Twelve Apostles at sunrise or sunset, when the light is best and the crowds are thinner; Port Campbell is the closest base. Book stays early for summer and long weekends.

regions.name: Grampians
regions.label: Grampians
regions.intro: The Grampians (Gariwerd) is a national park of sandstone ranges about three hours west of Melbourne, known for its lookouts, waterfalls such as MacKenzie Falls, spring wildflowers and Aboriginal rock art.
body: Halls Gap, in the middle of the park, is the main base, with kangaroos grazing on the town oval at dusk. Dunkeld, at the southern end, is the gateway to Mount Abrupt and Mount Sturgeon walks.
Check Parks Victoria for track and road closures before you go, especially after fires or heavy rain.

regions.name: Gippsland
regions.label: Gippsland
regions.intro: Gippsland covers Victoria's east: Phillip Island and the Bass Coast, the Gippsland Lakes, one of the largest inland waterway networks in Australia, and the remote beaches and forests of East Gippsland.
body: Phillip Island and Inverloch are an easy weekend from Melbourne. Further east, Lakes Entrance, Metung and Bairnsdale are a base for boating, fishing and quiet beaches, a three- to four-hour drive away.
Wilsons Promontory, the southernmost point of mainland Australia, is in South Gippsland and one of the state's most loved national parks.

regions.name: Bellarine Peninsula
regions.label: Bellarine Peninsula
regions.intro: The Bellarine Peninsula sits across the bay from the Mornington Peninsula, about 90 minutes from Melbourne via Geelong, with historic Queenscliff, family beaches at Ocean Grove and Barwon Heads, and cool-climate wineries.
body: Queenscliff has grand old hotels and a fort; Ocean Grove and Barwon Heads have the surf and river beaches. The Searoad ferry links Queenscliff with Sorrento for a loop of both peninsulas.

regions.name: High Country
regions.label: High Country
regions.intro: Victoria's High Country is the alpine north-east: the ski resorts of Mount Hotham, Falls Creek and Mount Buller in winter, and in summer rail trails, rivers and wineries around Bright, Beechworth and Mansfield.
body: Bright is the most popular base, with the Great Alpine Road climbing from Harrietville to Mount Hotham. Beechworth and Myrtleford add gold-era history and food, and Mansfield is the gateway to Mount Buller and Lake Eildon.
In winter, alpine roads may require snow chains: check VicRoads and the resorts before you drive. Autumn colours around Bright are a highlight from April.
